title: The Sydney Opera House
objective: After this level you can describe its sail-like roofs and how they were built.
summary: Utzon's winning shells took years to make buildable, until every shell was cut from one sphere, so the roof could be made of standard parts. Utzon resigned in 1966; the building opened in 1973.

cards.headline: In 1957, Jørn Utzon won a competition with a roof nobody knew how to build.
cards.body: The Danish architect's design beat 233 entries in the international competition for a Sydney opera house. It showed a cluster of sail-like shells rising over the harbor. Beautiful, and for years, impossible.

cards.headline: Every shell, cut from one sphere
cards.body: To build a shell, the engineers at Arup needed its shape as mathematics. From 1958 to 1962, Utzon's team tried parabolas, then ellipses, and neither worked. By late 1961 Utzon saw the key: every shell could be cut from the surface of a single sphere. One shared curve meant the roof could be split into standard parts, prefabricated and assembled on site. Picture every piece of a peel coming from the same ball.

mascot.line: When every curve is different, nothing repeats. Make them all one curve, and suddenly you have a kit.

cards.fact: The famous orange story is a myth.
cards.context: Popular legend says Utzon peeled an orange and saw the roof. The Sydney Opera House itself calls that a popular myth. An orange can show how the geometry works, but the breakthrough was Utzon noticing that the shells were so alike that one form, a sphere, could produce them all.

cards.headline: The architect who never came back
cards.body: The shells were solved; the politics were not. In February 1966, after a dispute with the New South Wales government, Utzon resigned, and a team led by Peter Hall took over the design. Utzon left Australia that April and never returned to see his building finished. It was completed in 1973 and joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2007.
